“I think I evened the score a bit while you were out, you know,” Phainon calls over his shoulder.
Still no response from Mydei, only the sound of corrupted flesh tearing. Phainon supposes that in itself is response enough. He yanks his sword from the neck of his last opponent and stands, trying to catch his breath. Yet his uneasiness lingers still, rising thickly into his throat.
The hairs on the back of his neck rise as his instincts scream at him to move. Corruption surges towards him from behind, and he tightens his hand on the hilt of his sword once more, whirling on his attacker—
—and he stabs Mydei straight through the upper chest, just beneath his collarbone.

Phainon and Mydei investigate a village drowned by the black tide. When Mydei falls, something else gets back up.

chapters.html:
Tragedy announced itself the way it often does: in the past tense, via a pair of battered survivors staggering through the front gates of Okhema in the early hours of the morning.

The younger of the two, a girl, was shaken but physically unharmed, dragging a half-conscious teenage boy draped over her shoulders. A large black-and-white dog covered in deep scratches limped ahead of them. It had circled the two children, growling softly, until the little girl coaxed it into the healers’ chamber at Hyacine’s behest.

When Mydei and Phainon left the city, the boy had yet to regain consciousness, and Hyacine’s expression was grim as she saw them off. The little girl and her dog were still waiting at the foot of her brother’s bed, watching the two men leave with hollow eyes.

Neither of them say it out loud as they approach the ruined village, but they do not expect this to be much of a rescue mission. Phainon, at least, finds it easier to look at this sort of thing primarily as clearing out the black tide. The lack of lives to save gets less oppressive that way.

The smell of it grows stronger as they get closer, cloying and metallic and thick enough that it seems to rest on the back of Phainon’s tongue like bile. It churns his stomach, makes his breath burn his throat. From the way Mydei’s scowl deepens, he can tell he isn’t alone in his discomfort.

They make their way towards the main road. A decent number of the storefronts there are still intact, boxes of vegetables and dried fruit untouched, jewelry hanging from mannequins catching the late afternoon light and casting kaleidoscope shadows back through the windows. Trickles of the black tide glisten like oil in the cracks between otherwise unharmed cobblestones. It must have blazed through this village so quickly that people didn’t have enough time even to panic; whether or not this is a sort of mercy, Phainon can never say.

“It was a nice place,” Phainon mumbles, half to himself. Mydei grunts in lieu of a response, but when Phainon looks back at him, his expression is dark and heavy as he eyes a fallen flower basket, crushed petals trailing down the street.

“You take the residential district,” says Mydei. “Circle around and meet me in the square.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow, smirking slightly despite himself. “Trying to take all the glory for yourself again?”

“Work quickly enough and there might be a few left for you by the time you get there.”

“Such magnanimity.”

“I’m known for it.”

“So I’m told.”

Mydei snorts. “Just watch your back, Deliverer.”

Phainon waves him off and heads for the cluster of houses at the far end of the long main street. As he gets closer, he notices that some of them are multiple-story, two-family homes, reminding him a little of those that once stood in Aedes Elysiae. The black tide trickles down walls in rivulets, congealing into thicker streams as it mixes with the dirt of the footpaths connecting neighboring houses. Seeming to swallow even his footsteps, the dead silence makes Phainon’s ears ring.

The first one he enters has an ornate marble fountain at the center of the open area in the middle. Two corrupted bodies lie half submerged in the water, likely having attempted to alleviate the burning of the tidal infection that way. Phainon averts his eyes. 

It never gets easier, picking through the aftermath of doomed life. The way some of them fell while trying to escape the fever burning them alive, the way some of them lost their sanity before their lives and tore each other apart, leaving chunks of tide-corrupted flesh scattered around their bodies. Sometimes he can still make out the murmuring when he gets close enough, indicating that the tide has not yet released those bodies; for these, he stabs his blade through the spine and twists until the murmurs dissipate with a sigh of relief. 

He doesn’t find many still moving, though, which is often the case in high-density areas such as this. Most of the surviving corrupted flee, driven by the last animal instinct left behind in the body the tide has overtaken, which is almost universally fear. Phainon can’t decide if this makes him feel better or worse.

The last house he checks is deceptively intact. The front door is still on its hinges, and a vibrant assortment of potted herbs and flowers remains untouched on the windowsill. He pushes the door open, not allowing himself to hope for much. Inside, the signs of a struggle are clearer, and he can see that the back door has been torn open from the outside; still, the traces of the tide are more sparse than they were in the other buildings. The house is quiet, but not oppressively so, as though it’s merely waiting.

In the first bedroom, he steps over a pile of rubble and a dead black tide creature, crouching by a fallen bookcase. He doesn’t know exactly what he’s looking for, if he’s looking for anything at all, only that he’s found nothing in any of the abandoned houses thus far and the thought of returning to that empty-eyed little girl with equally empty hands makes his stomach twist. As this thought forms, his eyes fall on a small shape lying on the floor.

Phainon picks it up and dusts it off carefully. He finds himself holding a small stuffed chimera doll, miraculously intact but for a small tear on the right ear. And suddenly he remembers the little girl crying, when she had first arrived, about having left something she called “Red” behind. He had assumed she was referring to another pet, or a friend, but now that he’s looking at the little red chimera doll, he wonders. Either way, it’s better than nothing, so he tucks it into his pocket.

There’s a murmur behind him and his body reacts faster than his mind, swinging around sideways and stabbing his sword into the leg of the black tide creature that had lunged towards him. It’s the same one he had stepped over before, the one he assumed was dead—it staggers back, but doesn’t fall. It mumbles urgently to itself, almost seeming not to notice him.

“Garden…the water…why…is…”

Phainon pauses, narrowing his eyes. He glances out the open window, towards the fenced-in backyard where he can just barely make out what looks like an herb garden. He looks back at the creature gently swaying before him.

“That was your garden,” he says softly. “Wasn’t it?”

“Mine…MINE!”

The creature wails in agony and charges at him clumsily. This time he stabs it through the heart, and it gurgles and sighs before going still. He lets it fall to the floor and swallows hard.

He makes his way to the backyard, where a small herb and flower garden lies half-trampled. A watering can lies forgotten, likely dropped when the gardener was attacked. Scenes like this are so common. Moments in time shattered as they play out, something that once might have been happy or peaceful stuttering over and over with no release until it warps into horror. 

Picking up the watering can, he finds it still halfway filled. He hesitates briefly, then finishes watering the plants that remain. A few of the flowers and herbs are still whole, could still be preserved; Mydei might very well have ideas about how to transport them back to Okhema, but if he doesn’t, Castorice certainly will. 

Phainon doesn’t hear much movement as he heads back towards the town square, and he resigns himself to Mydei’s inevitable commentary about his efficiency leaving much to be desired. Somewhere at the root of the feeling he finds himself grateful for it; his meeting with the gardener has him seeing the people who used to be where the black tide creatures now stand, and though he’s long grown past the child who would allow such a thing to make him hesitate, he can’t pretend to enjoy it, can’t pretend knowing he’s putting them out of their misery is enough to keep him from feeling sick to his stomach.

Even as he thinks it, he hears a high-pitched screech as a quadripedal black tide creation comes charging from the direction of the square. It nearly catches Phainon off guard, but he catches himself on the back heel and twists his sword into the spot between its shoulder blades as it rushes past, pushing down until the frenzied murmuring fades into nothingness.

The first thing he notices is that the creature was already wounded, with great chunks of flesh missing from its back haunches as though it had been torn at by a clawed pair of hands. The second thing he notices is that its face and mouth are covered in golden blood.

Phainon’s stomach drops. 

He tears towards the square, acutely aware of the way his boots break the silence with every strike against the stone-paved street. If Mydei has fallen—which must be what happened, otherwise he would never allow that thing to escape—Phainon has no idea how long ago that might have been, or what the remaining black tide might have done to his body in the meantime. He feels nauseous.

At first he doesn’t see Mydei at all, casting frantically between the overturned stalls. Then, a flash of red and gold catches his eye, nearly sunken into a pool of black tide near a fallen fruit stand. 

“Mydei!”

He scrambles towards the pool and grabs Mydei’s arm, ignoring the way his throat closes when Mydei doesn’t grip him back, how the tide prickles at his skin even through his gloves. Slowly, painstakingly, he pries Mydei’s body out of the black tide, slinging an arm over his shoulder and laying him carefully on the cobblestones. Automatically, he feels for a pulse, but he already knows Mydei’s gone; the head wound he’s sustained has crushed almost the entire right side of his skull, and his face is pale and bloodless. 

Phainon exhales shakily. This part, he will never be able to take in stride. 

Still, Mydei’s frowning face comes to memory, along with the reprimand he had given Phainon the last time he had fallen in the field. It was a waste of time, he chastised. It didn’t serve their purposes, and what he would prefer is for Phainon to stay focused. 

For now, the best he can do is protect Mydei’s body until he returns from the riverbank. Another wave of murmuring footsteps sweeps down the alleyways that lead into the square, growing ever closer; time and danger will not wait for Phainon, and he cannot allow himself to wait for them. He lifts the body into a more secure position, ensuring that if he jerks or spasms upon waking he won’t reinjure himself, 

At the very least, protecting Mydei gives him a different goal to focus on. It sharpens his reflexes, clears his thoughts, and he cuts down the approaching tidal monsters with little issue, prioritizing those coming towards the side closer to the body with wide, sweeping slashes that slice through two or three at a time. He flings them away, silencing a cacophony of despairing whispers in a blink.

When he senses movement at his back, he feels a sharp pang of relief. He steps forward to give Mydei space to move. 

“That was quick.”

Mydei doesn’t respond, but Phainon hears him tear an airborne denizen of the tide straight out of its flight path, ripping it in half as though it’s made of paper. He cuts down a few more, notices the numbers are thinning.

“I think I evened the score a bit while you were out, you know,” he calls over his shoulder. 

Still no response, only the sound of corrupted flesh tearing. Phainon supposes that in itself is response enough. He yanks his sword from the neck of his last opponent and stands, trying to catch his breath. Yet his uneasiness lingers still, rising thickly into his throat. 

The hairs on the back of his neck rise as his instincts scream at him to move. Corruption surges towards him from behind, and he tightens his hand on the hilt of his sword once more, whirling on his attacker—

—and he stabs Mydei straight through the upper chest, just beneath his collarbone.

Time seems to freeze around him. He barely has time to register what’s happening before Mydei grabs the blade of his sword with both hands and pulls it further into his body with a guttural snarl. He uses the shortened space between them to kick Phainon hard in the stomach, sending him flying into a nearby storefront. 

Phainon crashes through the window, reflexively throwing up his arms to protect his face from the shards of glass. Dazed, he staggers to his feet. He shakes the glass from his hair and it falls to the ground with an incongruently delicate tinkle.

Through the shattered window, he watches Mydei wrench the sword from his chest and toss it carelessly to the side. It clatters across the stone briefly before coming to rest.

Something isn’t right.

Of course something isn’t right.

His movements, his expression, his posture, none of it is right.

And a voice in the back of Phainon’s head, one that belongs to him and doesn’t at all, tells him with cold certainty: That is not Mydeimos.

His skin is still that of a corpse, ashen, almost grayish in tone, and he’s holding himself all wrong, shoulders half-slumped as though he’s being held up by a single string running through his spine. A black, tar-like substance drips down his face, streaking from his intact eye like tears and from the head wound Phainon now sees hasn’t healed at all. Inside the wound, where Mydei’s right eye should be, is the unmistakable orange-and-black light of a black tide core.

Phainon inhales sharply and Mydei’s head swivels jerkily to look at him. His eye seems to flicker, buzzing with some sort of visual static. It burns into him, straining his vision as though he’s trying to stare at the sun.

He flings himself at Phainon, who once again fails to react in time, forced to resort to shielding his face and head once more as he’s thrown back through the shattered storefront. He hits the ground hard, pain blooming across the left side of his body. Rolling back onto his feet with a hiss, he casts around desperately, trying to remember which direction Mydei had thrown his sword.

All the while Mydei’s body stalks towards him with that awful, unnatural gait. He’s not in there at all, but something else certainly is.

A glint of steel underneath the overturned fruit cart catches Phainon’s eye and he dives for it, but Mydei is faster. He hurtles into Phainon’s side and knocks the wind out of him as they both slam to the ground. Fallen fruit bursts beneath them, releasing the heady scent of citrus. 

Phainon gasps for air, barely managing to twist out of the way of Mydei’s fist as his gauntlet punches into the stone inches from his head. As it tears back out, he feels shards of bloodstone slice into the skin of his cheek, searing with a sizzling afterburn he knows to be that of the black tide. He fumbles desperately for his sword, straining towards the haft lying just out of reach.

Mydei grips his neck with one hand to hold him still, black tears falling from his eyes and onto Phainon’s face. He raises his gauntlet, his expression frozen into one of deadly focus that Phainon knows all too well.

Phainon’s fingers close around cold steel and he sweeps the blade up and out, throwing Mydei off balance for long enough to get some traction and kick him off with both legs. He backs up slowly, and as he does, his eyes fall on the shards of bloodstone lying on the ground. With dismay, he realizes they are no longer the color of blood at all, but rather the same sickly faded orange as the ordinarily bright red markings covering Mydei’s body. 

The markings themselves still pulse from time to time, more like the throbbing of an infection than the steady beat of a heart. Mydei sways on his feet slightly, staring at Phainon without seeing him.

A chill shoots down Phainon’s spine that has nothing to do with the danger he now finds himself in. For all the times he’s had to see Mydei in pain, watched him be mangled and choked and bled until he stops moving, even for all the times it has fallen to Phainon to land the final blow just to cut the suffering short, he has never seen anything like this. And because he has never seen this, he doesn’t know: is Mydei still coming back? Can he come back, now that the black tide has taken his body?

All those dreams where Phainon waits besides his corpse for eternities on end, only for it to remain still and cold and empty—is this how they find him?

“Tide…rend…enough…”

Hearing Mydei’s voice speak like that, in that stilted, muttering manner of those overtaken by the black tide—it raises a tidal wave of pain and grief that tears through Phainon’s body, nearly knocking him to back to his knees. 

Mydei circles, catlike. He feints to one side before flitting in the other direction so quickly he almost seems to disappear—something Phainon always maintains he shouldn’t be able to do, all things considered—Phainon barely raises his sword in time to block the incoming flurry of blows, and even so they rain down with such intensity that they punch his sword back into his gloves, cutting through the leather and into his skin. 

At last, a shred of muscle memory returns to him. He slides in a half-circle at the moment of impact, allowing the blade to slice deeper into his palm in order to use Mydei’s momentum against him. Mydei tumbles forward a few steps before his head snaps around to stare unblinking at Phainon.

“E…nough,” he mumbles. “Enough. Enoughenoughenoughenough—”

He continues to repeat the word as he lunges towards Phainon once more, but Phainon is ready for him this time, and he ducks under Mydei’s gauntlet to drive an elbow into his stomach. Mydei falls back with a sputtering grunt, and now it’s Phainon with the opening, his sword at Mydei’s throat.

Only.

Only he doesn’t know what will happen if he kills Mydei in this condition. You don’t know he’s gone, whispers a little voice in the back of his head, defiant and hopeful. You don’t know that.

The instant of hesitation is all Mydei needs to lash out and grab his wrist, twisting it out and away with such force that it wrenches his shoulder clean out of the socket. This time Phainon does scream, a sound with more fear and anger in it than pain, even as light explodes behind his eyes and blinds him to every square inch of his body that isn’t his dislocated shoulder.

Mydei makes a garbled sound that isn’t remotely close to a word and wrenches Phainon’s arm even harder, making him cry out again. And then he says, in a slurred murmur: “Hesi…tate.”

Phainon lets out a furious howl as he snatches up his sword with his good arm and plunges it into Mydei’s side. A mixture of diluted golden blood and black tar pours from the wound. Mydei grimaces, though he makes no sound of pain, and it’s only when Phainon drives the blade even deeper that he finally releases his wrist.

Breathing heavily, Phainon stares at him. He knows that move. He knows that move because the specifics of it belong to Mydei alone—he’s used it on Phainon more times than he can count while sparring, though admittedly never with that sort of brutality. But it’s his. 

Learn the consequences of hesitation well, Deliverer.

Phainon narrows his eyes and raises his sword once more, blood pounding in his ears.

“Give him back,” he whispers.

Mydei’s head falls to the side slightly, as though he has a neck injury of some sort. He does not look at Phainon. The wound on his side is already closing—it’s already closing, knitting together with a sickly pattern of black veins spidering out from the scar. Like an infection.

“Deli…verer…”

Phainon’s mind goes blank. A gust of wind blows past, carrying with it the scent of crushed fruit. The cold voice that belongs to him says, if you die here, they will only desecrate his body further, and the quiet one whispers, if you die here, so does he.

He bites down on the hilt of his sword and grabs his elbow with his good arm, twists it back hard until his shoulder snaps back into the socket with a dizzying crunch. He raises his eyes back to Mydei’s face, and sees that the tidal core behind his eye is glowing brighter, pulsing orange petals beginning to unfurl from the center.

Phainon rushes forward, hammering Mydei with a series of rapid blows that strike his gauntlets with a metallic clang as he whirls to deflect. It’s almost imperceptible, the slightest slowing of reflexes that he sees there, such a miniscule difference it would fail to register with anyone who hadn’t been hand-to-blade with him hundreds of times over.

Is he…getting worn out? Mydei would never wear out this quickly—but this isn’t Mydei, he reminds himself. Not really.

His second-long pause earns him a fist to the chest, and he nearly loses his footing again, but before he can fall he stabs his sword up and through Mydei’s forearm, using the leverage it gives him to keep his balance. Mydei’s body shudders; he tears his arm free with an awful squelching sound and a spray of black ooze, but the movement is jerky, stilted.

“Can’t…way…back,” he mumbles. “Breathe…can’t…”

“Yes, you can,” croaks Phainon, “yes, you can,” and he doesn’t know if Mydei can even hear him—his vacant eyes suggest otherwise, but the expression on his face has twisted into one Mydei very rarely wears: fear.

Suddenly Mydei screams wordlessly, the sound raw with equal parts terror and fury. He dives at Phainon, who manages to deflect one savage blow with his blade but immediately takes another hard hit to his wounded shoulder that makes him falter slightly as pain bursts back to the forefront. But Mydei doesn’t pounce on the opening the way he should, instead jerking halfway forward as though doing so was his intention before rocking back again on his heel, his arm half-raised as he mutters the word “no” over and over again.

Whatever resistance was there breaks, and he lunges into another attack. This time, Phainon lets him get close, until the feverish heat of the infection feels as though it could burn him with a touch, and then he slams his elbow as hard as he can into the side of Mydei’s head. It snaps back and Mydei staggers with a wordless snarl. Eyes unfocused, he stands very still, his visible pupil dilating and constricting as he breathes raggedly.

“Don’t…want,” he pants. “Want…please. Please.”

Phainon takes a deep breath.

“...Okay.”

Mydei is definitely slowing down now, faltering, missing opportunities he would never fail to take advantage of, occasionally jerking away with a pained spasm only to throw himself back at Phainon twice as hard. He’s erratic, the black tar running freely from his eyes, streaking down his neck and chest. His wounds still close quickly, but not effectively; they reopen and bleed anew if he moves the wrong way, like lazily done sutures. 

The core pulses sickly orange in time with his movements. In terms of raw strength, he is unchanged, even as his accuracy continues to decline.

Even thus handicapped, he is uniquely difficult to pin down. They continue to trade blows as Phainon searches doggedly for the right angle, slowly but surely putting Mydei on the defensive. He has just started to think he might be able to take advantage of pure exhaustion when Mydei leaps forward with a sudden burst of new energy, barreling into him and knocking him onto his back—but he spasms again instead of anchoring himself, and Phainon twists out from underneath, flips their position so that he’s pinning Mydei to the ground with his full weight. Mydei thrashes wildly, attempting to claw at Phainon’s face like a trapped animal, but Phainon pins one arm to his side with his knee, stabs his sword straight through the palm of the other.

He wraps his hands around Mydei’s exposed throat and presses down, trying his best to ignore the sticky, almost staticky feeling of the tidal residue smeared across it. Mydei writhes beneath him, snarling, but Phainon grits his teeth and squeezees harder. It had been Mydei himself who had instructed him in this particular manner of knocking an opponent out in the first place, he remembers: cut off the airflow for just long enough that they lose consciousness, then release such as to avoid unnecessary damage from lack of oxygen. And take care not to crush the windpipe, Mydei had added offhandedly, should you desire their survival. 

Phainon leans forward, stomach churning at the sound of Mydei’s choked wheezing, his struggling growing weaker and weaker as his chest heaves for air he isn’t getting. 

“I’m sorry,” he whispers, lips nearly brushing Mydei’s forehead. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”

Mydei’s good eye flutters, then abruptly snaps open and stares straight at Phainon. The visual static that had been flickering through it disappears, and when Phainon looks into it he sees Mydei looking back.

He recoils slightly and in doing so lessens the pressure on Mydei’s throat. Before he can process what’s just happened there’s a fist in the front of his coat and he’s being tossed away like a ragdoll, head cracking against the brick wall of the alleyway. Blood flows hot down the back of his neck as his vision goes white. He attempts to regain his footing, but Mydei has already closed the distance. 

A clawed gauntlet wraps around Phainon’s neck and lifts him clean off his feet. He kicks uselessly at the air, gasping, the grip crushing his remaining strength. Armored fingertips slice into skin of his throat; this time, there will be no second chance.

The arm gripping him spasms. Darkness creeps in from the edges of his vision, his lungs ready to burst, but still he forces his eyes to stay open, forces himself to focus on Mydei, whose face is twisted into a mask of agony. Phainon reaches up and grabs at the wrist still holding him off the ground and Mydei’s head snaps up to look at him.

All at once, the clarity returns to Mydei’s eyes, followed swiftly by confusion, then horror. He begins to tremble violently as he reaches for his face with his free arm and sinks his fingers deep into the pulsing tidal core blooming behind his eye.

“Enough,” he hisses, and wrenches the core from his skull with the crunching sound of crumbling rock.

The gauntlet releases Phainon, who falls to the ground as his body shakes with sobbing coughs. Frantically, he looks up at Mydei.

Mydei drops the core and stomps on it, grinding it under his heel. It bursts like a piece of rotting fruit. He meets Phainon’s eyes and the ghost of a smirk plays across his face.

“...Heh.”

He collapses, lifeless once more.

Rubbing his neck, Phainon stares at him, half expecting him to spring back up again, but he just lies there, unmoving, the remnants of the black tide flowing from reopened wounds as though being rejected by his body.

Still shaking, Phainon drags himself over to Mydei’s body. Now that he has a moment to stop and breathe, he becomes acutely aware of just how badly his head is pounding, how sore his shoulder is, the stinging cuts covering his hands and neck. Hyacine’s frowning face appears crystal clear in his mind’s eye, and the thought almost makes him chuckle, only he can sense that will hurt too.

He pulls Mydei into his arms and leans back against the bricks. Cradling his shoulders, he carefully adjusts so that Mydei’s upper body rests across his lap, head anchored in place by his forearm. Even if he didn’t know that stabilizing the head and neck would make healing from a head wound easier, Phainon thinks he might need to have Mydei as close as possible anyway, just to keep from screaming. He’s still trembling, despite this. He hopes it won’t carry over.

Phainon leans forward and presses his forehead to Mydei’s. “I’ve got you,” he whispers. “Good luck on the way back.”

They both smell of sweat and blood; the warmth of the baths back in Okhema has rarely felt so distant. Phainon watches the black liquid drip from Mydei’s body, slower and slower until only a trace of gold remains, and at last the wounds begin to knit back together properly. It’s far from the first time he’s seen this happen, but he feels a sudden wave of selfish gratitude towards whichever force of fate or nature had chosen Mydei to receive a body tethered in such a way that allows him to find his way back where others could not. This scene could have been a different one, Phainon knows. Would have been a different one, were it anyone else. He doesn’t let himself linger on it, but neither does he let himself forget.

Still, Mydei’s injuries are extensive—both those he had sustained fighting the black tide and from fighting Phainon himself—and the healing process is slow, far slower than usual. Ten minutes pass, then thirty. The silence of the courtyard is broken only by Phainon’s ragged breathing and the conspicuous absence of Mydei’s, and it eventually becomes oppressive, heavy. To offset it, he begins to hum one of Cyrene’s old lullabies to himself, absently untangling a blood-matted knot in Mydei’s hair with his fingertips. It helps, a little. 

His mind wanders to the little garden at the other end of the village. He wonders if Mydei might take interest in any of the herbs there, or if Castorice might be able to salvage the crushed flowers into one of her dried flower crowns. Maybe some of them are medicinal—he has never been particularly good at identifying those by sight, but Hyacine would know. Possibly it could distract her from telling him off again, or at least mollify her a little.

Mydei’s braid has come mostly undone. Phainon frowns slightly. Sometimes this seems to bother him more than anything else when he wakes up; of course he wouldn’t say anything, but Phainon notices the restless way he runs his hand through his hair, rolls his neck uncomfortably as though the balance is off. Carefully he combs his fingers through the tangled strands, prising away the last congealed chunks of tidal residue, then does his best to fix the braid. 

It certainly can’t compare to Aglaea’s handiwork, but he has improved over the past few months after practicing on ribbons at Castorice’s suggestion. He had been kicking himself after accidentally commenting that it would be nice to practice on Castorice’s hair, given how long and pretty it is. However, the brief sadness that flickered across her face was quickly replaced by an almost mischievous expression that reminded him somewhat unnervingly of Cipher.

Actually, Phainon, braiding hair of different lengths does require different techniques. I think you’d find mine’s a bit too long for your aims.

She cut three lengths of ribbon, knotted them together at one end, and directed him to practice on that instead. He’s kept it in his coat pocket ever since, fiddling with it in those too-quiet moments when he doesn’t know what to do with his hands.

Gently, Phainon wipes the last of the tarry black tear tracks from Mydei’s face with the corner of his sleeve, careful not to disturb the still-healing head wound. He’s nearly in one piece again, could almost be sleeping but for the stillness of death hanging across his chest. Phainon forces himself to focus instead on continuing to gingerly run his fingers through Mydei’s knotted golden locks, methodically teasing out the remaining tangles and smoothing them back into place. He does his best not to pull too hard, though he knows Mydei can’t feel it, not wanting his scalp to be sore when he wakes. He loses track of time this way, humming quietly and keeping watch over Mydei’s body as he puts himself back together.

At last, Mydei sucks in a jerky breath, and his eyes flutter open. He makes an odd sound and convulses, curling in on himself, until Phainon presses a hand gently but firmly to the side of his face to stabilize him. 

“Easy,” he says softly. “I’ve got you.”

Mydei glances up at him and Phainon nearly lets out a sob of relief when he meets an intact pair of tired and somewhat disoriented golden eyes. With a groan, Mydei throws his arm over his face. “This is what being hungover feels like, isn’t it.”

Phainon laughs shakily. “I’d…imagine this is probably a little worse.”

With Phainon’s help, Mydei slowly manages to get upright and lean against the wall at his side. They don’t speak for a while, then, arms brushing together as they stare up at the swirls of pink and deep blue drifting across the sky. In that moment, to Phainon, the only sound in the world is the quiet, steady breathing of the man beside him. He thinks that if everything else were to disappear, he might be okay like this, staying here forever. But it won’t, and they can’t.

Finally, Mydei looks over at him critically. “You look terrible.”

“You should see the other guy.” Phainon smiles weakly. “Or, should have seen the other guy half an hour ago. Before he regenerated all of it.”

Mydei’s eyes flick from the deep scratches on Phainon’s neck to his bruised face and throat, the way he favors his shoulder. He shakes his head with a sigh. “Hyacine might really kill us this time.”

Phainon chuckles at that, but his smile quickly fades. “Mydei…what happened?”

“I…” Mydei furrows his brow, uncharacteristically hesitant. “I…I don’t know. There were three of them. One got my head in its mouth, that’s the last thing I…and then I…couldn’t get back in.”

He clearly has no desire to elaborate, and Phainon doesn’t press. “I didn’t know that could happen.”

“...Neither did I.” Mydei presses his lips together, jaw tight.

“I won’t let it do that to you again,” Phainon says fiercely. “You have my word.”

Mydei shakes his head again. “It won’t always be up to you, Deliverer.”

He’s right. Phainon knows he’s right, but the thought of once again being forced to watch the black tide puppet Mydei’s body like a piece of taxidermy still turns his stomach. He swallows. 

“Well, I…I’m glad you’re all right.”

“You did a decent job of not dying on me, for your part.”

“Decent?” Phainon scoffs. “I’d say it was more than decent.”

“Oh?” Mydei raises an eyebrow. “What was that at the end, then?”

“I—you—it caught me off guard.”

“Which is precisely what makes it only decent.”

A retort is half-formed on his tongue when he looks over at Mydei to find him smirking ever so slightly. Phainon rolls his eyes and laughs, then winces when the movement makes his cracked rib throb.

“...I have a question, if I may,” says Mydei.

Phainon touches his ribs gingerly, feeling for the offending bone. “So formal, all of a sudden.”

“That…song.”

He stiffens, eyes locked on the opposite wall. “I didn’t think you could hear that.”

“Only during the last stretch. I was wondering where it came from. It was…” Mydei pauses, seeming to struggle for the right word, then shrugs. “It was nice.”

Once again, Phainon finds himself caught off guard. He hesitates, unsure of what to say. “It’s—it’s just a lullaby from home. From Aedes Elysiae, I mean. My…my friend used to sing it to me.” He sighs quietly. “I’m probably the only one left who remembers it, anyway.”

“One of two, now,” corrects Mydei mildly, and Phainon blinks at him, taken aback.

“Yeah, I…I guess so.” He smiles, sheepish yet gratified as warmth blooms deep in his chest.

With a grunt, Mydei pushes himself to his feet. “Come on,” he says. “I’m just about sick of this place, and if we’re already doomed to an earful then we may as well get it over with.” 

He offers a hand to Phainon, who takes it and allows himself to be hoisted up. It calms him somewhat, feeling the strength returned to Mydei’s body firsthand—particularly because he himself is both incredibly sore and intensely dizzy, and he knows full well that is liable to affect his reflexes.

Mydei stretches, rolling his shoulders and cracking his neck. Absently he brushes his hair out of his face, then goes completely still as he catches his braid between his index and middle fingers. He stares over at Phainon, his expression unreadable.

Phainon’s cheeks burn. He begins to stammer something out, maybe an apology, maybe an explanation, but before he can decide what it is he wants to say Mydei has swiftly closed the distance between them and the words fade in his mouth under the heat of that burning gaze. He can only stand, transfixed as though by the sun, as Mydei takes his face in his hands and kisses him.

He tastes of rust and tears and the color gold. 

There’s a desperation to it that Phainon hadn’t caught in the space between his words, something between hunger and tenderness and ferocious, bloody desire. It doesn’t escape his notice that Mydei’s hands are trembling, and he knows it doesn’t escape Mydei’s that his are too. 

Even as he pushes Phainon back against the wall he’s gentle, pulling his lower back forward and pressing his palms up so that it doesn’t scrape on the brick. Phainon wraps his arms around Mydei’s waist and allows himself to melt into the embrace, exhaustion and relief making him weak at the knees. The moment is short, as they always are, but brevity does not diminish the warmth of it.

They pull apart but not away, foreheads resting together. Phainon kneads the small of Mydei’s back, pressing into warm skin with his fingertips, and Mydei lets out a soft sigh as he arches lightly into the touch. He reaches up to stroke Phainon’s cheekbone with his thumb, carefully avoiding the bruises.

“I was scared,” whispers Phainon, guiltily, like a confession. “I didn’t know if you were coming back.”

“I know.” Mydei closes his eyes and nods. “I didn’t, either, for a while there.”

Phainon tightens his arms around Mydei’s waist. “But you did.”

“Yes, I did.”

He buries his face in Mydei’s neck, breathing in the familiar smell of spice and honey that lingers even beneath the layers of blood and sweat. Mydei is warm, and he’s alive, and his pulse beats steadily as he traces soothing patterns through Phainon’s hair. For a moment, even amidst the horror of the black tide and the fears they both hide, they are together, and they are safe.

Mydei rests his chin on the top of Phainon’s head briefly before finally pulling away. “Let’s go, then.”

Phainon nods and starts to follow him out of the alleyway before he abruptly remembers the garden. It feels like days ago that he’d been holding that watering can, though he knows it can’t have been more than a few hours in reality. “Hold on—wait.”

Mydei turns, raising an eyebrow in silent curiosity. 

“There was a house back there—it had this little garden, just, you know, herbs and flowers and things like that. I thought…I thought—I mean, some of it was still intact, so I thought we might be able to…bring a little bit back. For those kids.”

Mydei folds his arms across his chest, considering. “This house,” he says slowly. “Did it have a kitchen? Pots and the like?”

“I’d…assume so?”

“All right.” He nods. “Lead the way, then.”

//

“He’s been—oh, watch your step, there.”

Phainon picks his way around a cluster of crates, noting an assortment of multicolored jars and parchment paper. “What are these for?”

“Hm?” Hyacine glances back. “Reagents. I want to try a few things with those herbs you brought back.”

“You think they’ll be able to help anyone?”

“Oh, I’m certain they will.” She nods emphatically. “The rosemary especially, if we can get it to keep growing. It has excellent anti-inflammatory qualities that I’m sure I can enhance with some additional ingredients.”

He chuckles. “That’s…a little beyond my field of expertise, but I’m glad to hear it.”

“Here, this way.”

She leads him up a set of wide marble stairs, towards the double doors that open up into the infirmary wing where the two children have been resting. On Hyacine’s orders, there are only a few healers attending to the area, and the quiet click of their footsteps against the floor echoes in the stillness.

“The older brother regained consciousness this morning,” she says. “His name is Dimitri, his sister’s is Sophia. She’s been much more talkative since he woke up.”

“How is he?”

“Still quite weak. I don’t expect he will be up and about for at least another few days.”

Even so, the light in her eyes gleams far brighter than it had when Mydei and Phainon left for the village. Unlike then, she is clearly optimistic about his chances now.

“Speaking of the herbs, actually,” Phainon says, “Mydei and Castorice have finished repotting them. There are some flowers we didn’t recognize, too, so we figured you might want to take a look at them. You know, just in case.”

“Oh, that’s perfect, actually.” She smiles warmly. “It’s been such a long time since I got to work with anything new.”

“If you’re happy, I’m happy.”

Her smile fades slightly as she looks at him, a slight crease appearing between her brows. “And how are you feeling? How’s your head?”

“Mine?” He blinks. “Still attached, last I checked.”

“Phainon.” Hyacine frowns at him. “Be serious. That was a nasty concussion you walked in with.”

“I’m fine.” He raises his hands in surrender when she narrows her eyes further. “Really. I just needed some rest.”

She levels a piercing look at him that so closely resembles the one he had seen in his mind’s eye that Phainon has to suppress a grin. “Remember the symptoms I told you to watch out for. We don’t want you getting permanent brain damage because you were too stubborn to admit it.”

“Yes, doctor.”

Hyacine stops in the doorway and turns around, blocking the entrance and gazing up at Phainon with a serious expression. “Mydei told me what happened.”

Phainon grimaces. “Ah.”

“He wanted to know if there would be any lingering effects on his body.”

Shit. He hadn’t even thought of that. “Will there be?”

She shakes her head. “Not that I can anticipate. His system seems to have taken on the expulsion of the remaining tidal traces as part of the full healing process once the core was removed. But…”

He tenses, but Hyacine hesitates, her eyes flicking back down the hallway in the direction from which they’d come. “But?”

“I just…” She bites her lip. “I…I don’t know. He’s a special case, you know that. He always has been. I just feel like sometimes…”

The words trail off into silence. Phainon can hear what sounds like a group of small children scampering past outside, shouting and laughing in the sunlight he knows lies beyond these walls.

“...I guess I’m just glad you were there,” Hyacine says at last, voice soft. “I think you might have saved him from something that could’ve been…bad.”

Phainon presses his lips together and nods, not trusting the tightness in his chest enough to speak. Hyacine smiles and places a gentle hand on his arm.

“Keep having his back, okay?”

“Always,” Phainon whispers fiercely. “I swear. Always.”

She nods, satisfied with his response, and moves to the side, allowing him to pass into the treatment area. The young girl’s head whips around as soon as they cross the threshold, her eyes brightening when she recognizes Phainon. 

“Look, Dimitri, that’s him!” She grabs her brother’s hand. “He’s one of the ones who went back home!”

The boy named Dimitri looks up at Phainon with sunken eyes, his gaunt face and exhausted expression painfully familiar. Phainon takes a deep breath and tries to smile as he kneels beside the bed.

“Hey,” he says quietly. “Sorry it took us so long.”

The girl—Sophia—shakes her head hard. “No, don’t say sorry.”

“You got hurt,” the boy croaks, and Phainon winces slightly, rubbing his bandaged neck. 

“This? Oh, that’s nothing.” He winks. “You should see the other guy.”

The little girl giggles. Phainon feels something wet brush against his hand and looks down to see their dog poking its large head out from underneath Dimitri’s bed, where it had apparently been hiding. It noses curiously at his knuckles. He scratches behind velvety ears and the dog wriggles out further, tongue lolling happily.

“Ah, before I forget—I have something for you.”

He pulls the battered chimera plushie from his pocket and the little girl’s eyes go wide.

“It’s a little worse for wear, but I remembered you—”

The girl cuts him off before he can finish, letting out a high-pitched shriek of joy as she hugs the doll tightly to her chest. 

“You found her!” she cries. “I can’t believe you really found her!”

“I have a friend who would be happy to stitch her torn ear,” Hyacine pipes up, glancing up from the stack of medicinal tinctures she’s been organizing as they speak. “She’s probably too shy to tell you, but she’s knitted some chimera-sized sweaters that will keep your friend nice and cozy, too.”

“Really?” Sophia beams, practically bouncing in her seat. “Do you hear that, Red? Did you hear her?”

Hyacine laughs. “Yes, really.”

She continues to smile as she’s introduced to “Red”, listening to Sophia’s happy chattering with warm eyes.

“...Thank you, sir.”

The boy’s voice is soft, almost a whisper.  “Please. It’s just Phainon.”

“You…” Dimitri hesitates, chewing the inside of his cheek. “You didn’t…find anyone. Did you.”

It isn’t a question, not really. Phainon shakes his head slowly. “I’m sorry.”

The boy inhales, closes his eyes tight. Phainon can see his hands trembling, and his heart aches like an old wound.

“You know…” He pauses. “You know, when I was your age, the black tide got my home too.”

Dimitri looks up at him. “Does it ever…stop feeling like this?”

“No.” He knows well how lies can soothe, as well as the damage they can do. “But you learn to feel other things, too. With enough time.”

The boy’s lip trembles, but he doesn’t cry. He gazes at his sister with wordless grief. “She’s not even seven yet, you know. Her birthday’s next month.”

“Is it, now?” Phainon raises an eyebrow, smiling. “I know a guy who bakes a killer pomegranate tart, if you want to do something to celebrate.”

“I…yeah, actually. I think she’d like that a lot.” 

Dimitri’s expression grows almost imperceptibly lighter. Having something to look forward to, even something small—when your life shatters in your hands, the future can feel as though it, too, has been torn away. A reminder that there will still be a tomorrow, and then a next day, even when the thought of reaching them seems too painful to stomach; time, with equal parts cruelty and compassion, does not pause for grief.

“And,” Phainon says gently, “you need to remember that it wasn’t your fault.”

“It feels like it was,” mumbles Dimitri, still looking at his sister. “It feels like I’m here ‘cause they’re not.”

“I know. But, listen—Sophia’s alive because you’re still here, you know? You even got out with this guy,” he adds, scratching the top of the dog’s head. The dog thumps his back leg against the floor, as though in emphatic agreement. “That’s more than a lot of people.”

“...No one got out with you, did they?”

He looks up to find Dimitri watching him intently, and flashes a sad smile.

“No,” he says. “No, no one did.”

Muffled voices by the door draw his attention. Phainon turns to see Mydei and Hyacine carrying a pair of medium-sized window planters, with Castorice trailing quietly behind. Hyacine murmurs something to Mydei and he nods, taking the planter from her hands and setting both of them on the windowsill nearest to Dimitri’s bed.

Sophie gasps, her eyes round. Her brother says nothing, but his face pales slightly, as though the hope on hers frightens him.

“These were the only plants we could salvage,” Mydei explains, leaning back against the wall with folded arms, “but Castorice is working on pressing the flowers that didn’t make it.”

Castorice nods. “Um, I can bring them to you when they’re—I mean, if you’d like to have them, you can.”

The girl’s lip trembles as she runs a finger across the painted rim of one of the planters, tracing the carefully inked patterns of scales and stars. One holds a sparse but healthy assortment of leafy herbs, the other a handful of flowers in varying states.

“This is really pretty,” she murmurs.

“Cas painted them herself,” Hyacine interjects proudly, and Castorice blushes. Sophia smiles at her.

“Thank you, miss, Mama would—”

Her voice catches, and Phainon can make out the telltale glint of tears in her eyes as she quickly turns away from her brother, who pretends not to notice.

“It was our mother’s herb garden,” he says hoarsely. “The flowers were—they were our dad’s. She kept taking care of them after he died, it was…it was really important to her.” He swallows, looking back at his sister. “Mom was—she was outside when they came, she told us to run, I didn’t—I figured it would be—”

He stops himself. The dog whines softly, moving to rest its head on his leg. 

“Thank you,” Dimitri whispers. “It means a lot to—to both of us. To all of us.”

“You’ll return one day.”

Mydei’s words weigh heavily in the sudden quiet as he fixes his gaze on the boy before him.

“You’ll return,” he repeats, “and you will replant your mother’s garden in a world after the black tide that took her from you. For now, though, your duty is to safeguard what remains until that day comes. Both of you. Do you understand this?”

Dimitri nods silently. 

“Do you really think that?”

Sophia turns back around, glaring fiercely at Mydei with unshed tears still shining in her eyes. 

“Do you really think we’re gonna get to go back, because, I, I don’t want you to say it at all if you don’t really think it.”

“Sophia,” Dimitri says sharply.

She doesn’t react, still staring at Mydei with her little hands balled into fists at her side. "Tell me the truth," she demands.

He looks back at her evenly for a long moment, then slowly nods before lowering his eyes to meet Phainon’s with a gaze so full of certainty and faith it seems to settle somewhere deep in his chest, burning bright as the sun.

“Yes,” says Mydei. “Yes, I do.”
